newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: FLOODS CUT CZECH TAX TAKE CZK 10 BLN-FINMIN QUOTED.
newsitem.headline: FLOODS CUT CZECH TAX TAKE CZK 10 BLN-FINMIN QUOTED.

text.p: Recent floods in the Czech Republic will likely result in tax collection more than 10 billion crown lower than expectations, the CTK news agency quoted Finance Minister Ivan Pilip as saying on Monday.

The minister said the floods, which have devastated low-lying areas in the east the past two weeks, were lowering the chances to keep the state budget in balance this year, as tax collection from afflicted companies would slump.

"The room of the government to take some steps to (the budget's) balance is very limited at this moment," Pilip told CTK. The types of taxes and the budget period Pilip was referring to was not made clear.
The minister rejected suggestions that stat finances would slip into deficit next year. "The budget for 1998 will be planned as at least balanced," he said.
The central bank has called for a surplus budget in 1997 and 1998 in order to slow down aggregate demand which is contributing to the country's growing current account deficit.
Trade and current account deficits triggerred a run on the crown which forced the central bank to float the currency in May.
The rain-induced floods swept away some 1,500 houses and damged thousands. Rail and road links were cut, as well as telephone service and power and gas supplies.
Large number of companies were forced to shut down or cut production doe to the disaster. Total preliminary damage estimates have been put at 50 to 100 billion crowns.
Some areas were still under water on Monday despite easing of the rain.
After the crown was floated the government adopted a second series of budget cuts in as many months to compensate for a slowdown of budget revenues, while reducing demand.
The government and the parliament have approved the issuing of up to five billion in flood bonds, and released some six billion in other funds to help the flooded areas.
